title: Grace and cooperation
hook: Catholics stress grace that heals and lifts, and our free cooperation with it

segments.voice: Yesterday, theosis: iron in the coals, glowing all through and still iron. Your line was iron in the fire. What warmth did you stay near? Day one thousand ninety.

Halfway through a sentence, Paul changes his mind about who did the work. He's writing to the church in Corinth about his years on the road, and it starts out sounding like a boast: "I laboured more abundantly than they all." Then he catches himself, right there on the page: "yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me." So which is it? Did Paul work harder than the other apostles, or did grace do it? He seems to say both, in the same breath, and he doesn't feel any need to choose. That little correction is a doorway into how Catholics talk about being saved. Today's word: grace and cooperation.
screen: `YET NOT I, BUT THE GRACE OF GOD.`

segments.voice: Grace is God's free gift of his own help and life. In Catholic teaching, it comes first, always. Nobody earns the start. But grace doesn't push a person around like a chess piece. It heals the will and lifts it, so that the person can freely say yes, and keep saying it. That's cooperation: working together. Paul uses that very idea in his first letter to Corinth: "For we are labourers together with God." Together. And that is the shape of his correction in the hook: I worked hard, yet not I. Not half and half, like two people splitting a bill. More like a sail and the wind. The wind does the moving. The sail still has to be raised. Catholic teaching points to Mary as a picture of this. An angel brings her an astonishing message, and she asks a real question: "How shall this be?" Then she answers: "be it unto me according to thy word." Grace came first, to her. Her yes was still her own. Augustine, in a sermon, put it in a way tradition still repeats: the God who made you without you will not justify you without you. Protestants, as we heard two days ago, stress that faith itself is a gift so that no one can boast, and they guard against anything that sounds like earning. Catholics answer that our yes is itself a fruit of grace. Both are protecting the same thing: it all starts with God.

Here's the practice: cooperate with one grace today. Settle, and breathe. Think of one gift you already have and didn't make yourself: a steady hand, a good ear, a way with words, a free hour this afternoon. Pick one. In this teaching, that's a place where grace has already been at work. Now think of one person today who could use it, and what using it for them would look like: one call, one meal, one hour. Keep it small and real. If you pray, you can offer that gift back to God and ask for help to use it. If you don't, just settle on the person and the step. The bell holds the time.
Grace and cooperation. God's gift comes first, healing and lifting the will, and the person freely works together with it.
Your line: grace and yes. Take the small step you chose before the day ends. Raise the sail, and let the wind do the moving. Day one thousand ninety.

howItsDone: Catholics receive grace above all through the sacraments, such as baptism, confession and the Eucharist, and in the Angelus and the rosary they repeat Mary's words, be it done unto me according to thy word, as a pattern of saying yes to God.
